Use knowledge of Greek-origin prefixes (auto-, tele-, micro-) and Latin-origin prefixes (inter-, trans-, sub-) to decode and define unfamiliar vocabulary in context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} comes across an unfamiliar word containing a Greek or Latin root they recognise — like "port" in "transport" or "bio" in "biology" — can they use that to work out the meaning?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Idioms & Proverbs
topics.description: Recognise and interpret common idioms (break the ice, hit the nail on the head), adages (actions speak louder than words), and proverbs (a stitch in time saves nine), understanding their figurative meanings and when to use them
evidence: Explain the figurative meaning of common idioms encountered in texts, e.g. 'let the cat out of the bag' means to reveal a secret, not literally releasing a cat
Interpret the meaning and intended lesson of adages and proverbs, e.g. explain that 'the early bird catches the worm' advises that acting promptly gives an advantage
Use context clues to determine the meaning of an unfamiliar idiom or proverb encountered during reading and verify using a reference source
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears a saying like "don't judge a book by its cover" or "the early bird catches the worm," do they know what it really means and when you'd use it?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Similes & Metaphors
topics.description: Understand and identify similes (comparisons using like or as) and metaphors (direct comparisons stating something is something else) in texts, explaining how each creates imagery and conveys meaning
evidence: Identify similes in a text by locating comparisons using 'like' or 'as' and explain what two things are being compared and what quality is highlighted, e.g. 'The snow was like a white blanket'
Identify metaphors in a text and explain the implied comparison, e.g. in 'Time is a thief', explain that time is compared to a thief because it takes things away
Explain how a simile or metaphor in a poem or story creates a particular image or feeling for the reader that a literal description would not achieve
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a description like "the moon was a silver coin" or "her smile was like sunshine," can they explain what image the author was trying to create?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing Formal Vocabulary
topics.description: Distinguish between formal and informal vocabulary, selecting words appropriate for formal speech and writing such as 'discover' instead of 'find out' and 'request' instead of 'ask for'
evidence: Replace informal words with formal equivalents in a given text
Identify formal vocabulary choices in official letters and reports
Write the same message twice using formal vocabulary for a letter and informal vocabulary for a text message
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is writing something formal — like a letter or a report — do they choose more sophisticated words, like "enquire" instead of "ask" or "sufficient" instead of "enough"?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Dialects & Registers
topics.description: Compare and contrast the varieties of English used in stories, dramas, or poems, including dialects and registers, understanding how language varies by region, context, and purpose
evidence: Identify dialect features in character dialogue and explain their effect
Compare formal and informal registers in different types of texts
Explain how an author uses language variety to develop character or setting
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} reads a story with characters who speak in dialect or old-fashioned language, can they understand it and explain how it differs from the way we speak today?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Using a Thesaurus to Choose Words
topics.description: Use a thesaurus to find synonyms and extend vocabulary choices, selecting the most appropriate word based on context, connotation, and register
evidence: Use a thesaurus to find three alternatives for overused words in own writing
Select the most appropriate synonym from thesaurus options based on context and tone
Explain why one synonym is more suitable than another for a specific sentence
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is writing and wants a better word than the one they first thought of, can they use a thesaurus and pick the right synonym for the context — not just any word that means something similar?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Responding to Writing Feedback
topics.description: With teacher guidance, re-read own writing aloud to check it sounds right; listen and respond to questions and suggestions from teacher or peers to add detail, clarify meaning, and strengthen writing — this is the scaffolded beginning of writing self-evaluation, not an independent skill
evidence: Reread own writing and spot a missing word or unclear sentence
Add a detail in response to a question (e.g. 'Can you tell me more about...?')
Make at least one improvement to a piece based on feedback
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s teacher asks them to read their own writing aloud and then asks "does that bit make sense?", can {{name}} listen to the feedback and make a simple change to improve it?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Saying Sentences Before Writing Them
topics.description: Say out loud what is going to be written; compose sentences orally before writing them down as preparation for independent writing
evidence: Say a complete sentence aloud before attempting to write it
Rehearse a sentence orally more than once to hold it in memory
Practise sentences with a partner before writing independently
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts writing a sentence, do they say it out loud first — testing how it sounds — before putting pen to paper?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Shared Research Projects
topics.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects; recall information from experiences or gather information from sources to answer a question
evidence: Contribute ideas and information to a class writing project
Draw or write facts learned from personal experience about a topic
Help gather information from books or adults for a group research task
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is given a writing project that involves finding out about something — like an animal or a place — can they look up information and use what they find to write about the topic?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Sharing and Publishing Your Writing
topics.description: Read own writing aloud clearly enough to be heard by peers and the teacher; use digital tools to produce and publish writing
evidence: Read own sentences aloud with clear voice and appropriate expression
Share a piece of writing by reading it to the class
Type simple words or sentences using a computer or tablet
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read their own writing aloud to the class clearly enough for everyone to hear and follow along — and have they ever typed or published a piece of writing using a computer or tablet?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Simple Stories with Beginning and Ending
topics.description: Write simple narratives by sequencing sentences to describe events in order; narrate a single event or linked events with a beginning, middle, and ending or reaction
evidence: Write a short story with at least three sequenced sentences
Use time words like 'first', 'then', 'next' to order events
Include a reaction or ending to a narrative (e.g. 'I felt happy')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a short story about something that happened — with a clear beginning, middle, and end — so that someone who wasn't there could follow what happened and in what order?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing opinions
topics.description: Compose opinion pieces using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic or book and state a preference or opinion about it
evidence: State an opinion clearly (e.g. 'My favourite animal is a dog because...')
Give at least one reason for an opinion
Draw, dictate, or write to express a preference about a book or topic
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a sentence or two giving their opinion about something — like their favourite book or food — and explain why they feel that way?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Process Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of the writing process — compose, plan, draft, revise, edit, proofread, genre, audience, purpose, narrative, recount, instruction, paragraph, sequence, and detail — and understand that these words describe distinct steps and decisions that all writers make, not just tasks to tick off
evidence: Use 'compose', 'revise', and 'edit' correctly when describing the stages of writing
Explain who the 'audience' is for a piece of writing and how that changes what they write
Describe the purpose of a piece of writing (to persuade, inform, entertain, or instruct) and match their language to it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you asked {{name}} to explain what they're doing when they write a story at school, could they walk you through each step using words like 'plan', 'draft', and 'revise' — showing they understand it's a process, not just one sitting?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing to inform
topics.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts using drawing, dictating, or writing that name a topic and supply some information about it
evidence: Write or dictate two or three facts about a familiar topic
Label diagrams or drawings with informative details
Name a topic and provide relevant details about it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a few sentences explaining something they know about — like how butterflies grow or how to make a sandwich — naming the topic and sharing some facts?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Basic Informational Writing
topics.description: Compose informative or explanatory texts that introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section
evidence: Write an informative text that introduces a topic clearly and groups related information together
Use facts, definitions, and concrete details to develop and explain points about the topic
Provide a concluding statement or section that wraps up the information presented
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an explanatory or informative piece — like "How Volcanoes Work" — that introduces the topic clearly, develops it with facts and definitions, and ends with a conclusion?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Building Writing Stamina
topics.description: Write about real events and for different purposes, developing stamina for sustained writing across genres beyond narrative (e.g., recounts, letters, instructions)
evidence: Write a recount of a school trip using temporal connectives (first, then, after that)
Write a simple set of instructions with numbered steps
Sustain writing for an extended period across a full page without stopping
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write in different styles for different purposes — for example, writing a recount of a school trip, a letter to a friend, or a set of instructions for a game?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Planning Ideas Before Writing
topics.description: Plan before writing by saying aloud or noting down what will be written, writing down ideas and key words, and encapsulating ideas sentence by sentence before composing
evidence: Verbally rehearse sentences before writing them down
Jot key words or ideas in a planning format (e.g., story map) before drafting
Write a simple plan with beginning, middle, and end for a story
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they spend a few minutes planning — jotting down ideas, key words, or a rough structure — rather than jumping straight into writing the first sentence?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing
topics.description: Proof-read own writing to check for errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation; evaluate and revise writing with teacher/peer support, re-reading to ensure meaning is clear and tense is consistent
evidence: Re-read own writing and spot a missing full stop or capital letter
Identify and correct a tense inconsistency in a piece of writing
Discuss improvements with a partner and make at least one revision to strengthen the writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} finishes a piece of writing, do they proofread it for spelling mistakes, missing punctuation, and errors in grammar — and make corrections before handing it in?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Structured Opinion Writing
topics.description: Compose opinion pieces that introduce a topic, state a clear point of view, provide organised reasons linked with connecting words, and include a concluding statement or section
evidence: Write an opinion piece that introduces the topic, states a clear opinion, and provides at least two reasons
Use linking words (because, and, also, for example) to connect the opinion to supporting reasons
End an opinion piece with a concluding statement that restates or reinforces the opinion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write a persuasive piece — like arguing for a longer lunch break or why dogs are better pets than cats — with a clear viewpoint, organised reasons, and a conclusion?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Poetry
topics.description: Write poetry, exploring patterns of language, rhyme and rhythm, and learning poems by heart for recitation with appropriate intonation
evidence: Write a simple poem using rhyming couplets or a repeated pattern
Recite a poem from memory with expression and appropriate intonation
Identify rhyme and rhythm patterns in poems read aloud
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} tried writing a poem — playing with rhyme, rhythm, or repeating patterns — and can they recite one they've learned or written with expression?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Narrative Writing
topics.description: Write narratives with developed settings, characters and plot, using dialogue and description to develop experiences and show character responses to situations
evidence: Write a narrative that includes a described setting, at least one developed character, and a clear plot with a problem and resolution
Use dialogue to show what characters say and reveal their personality or feelings
Use descriptive details and temporal words to organise events into a clear sequence with a satisfying ending
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a story, do they bring it to life with descriptions of the setting, details about the characters, and some dialogue — rather than just listing what happened?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Organising Writing into Paragraphs
topics.description: Organise writing into paragraphs, grouping related material around a theme, and use simple organisational devices such as headings and sub-headings in non-narrative writing
evidence: Divide a piece of writing into paragraphs, each focused on one main idea or aspect of the topic
Use headings and sub-headings to organise a non-fiction text (e.g., a report about animals with sections 'Habitat', 'Diet', 'Appearance')
Identify where a new paragraph should begin in a given text and explain why (e.g., 'A new paragraph starts here because the topic changes from appearance to diet')
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a longer piece — like a report or a story — do they organise it into paragraphs, with related ideas grouped together and, where appropriate, headings to help the reader navigate?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Rehearsing and Varying Sentences
topics.description: Compose and rehearse sentences orally before writing, progressively building varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures including dialogue
evidence: Rehearse a sentence containing dialogue aloud before writing it (e.g. 'Let's go!' shouted Tom)
Orally compose sentences with varied openers (e.g. time adverbials, subordinate clauses) before writing
Try out two or three different ways to express the same idea orally and choose the most effective version to write
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} try out a sentence aloud before writing it — experimenting with different words and structures to find the version that sounds best?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing (age 7+)
topics.description: Evaluate and edit writing by assessing effectiveness, proposing changes to grammar and vocabulary for consistency, and proof-reading for spelling, grammar and punctuation errors at Y3-4 level
evidence: Read own or a peer's writing aloud and suggest specific improvements to vocabulary or sentence structure
Propose changes to grammar and word choice to improve clarity and consistency across a piece of writing
Proof-read writing at Y3-4 level for spelling, punctuation, and grammatical errors and correct them independently
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} revisits a draft piece of writing, can they improve it — changing word choices to be more precise, fixing inconsistent tenses, and correcting spelling and punctuation errors?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Revising and editing (age 8+)
topics.description: Read back your own writing critically and independently — notice where meaning is unclear, where a word could be stronger, or where the reader might be confused; make revisions without needing teacher prompts, using your own judgment about what is and isn't working
evidence: Reread a paragraph silently and independently identify at least one place where meaning could be clearer or a word choice improved
Make a revision that goes beyond spelling/punctuation — changing a sentence for clarity or effect
Explain in their own words why they changed something ('I thought the reader wouldn't understand what I meant')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read back something they've written — a story, a report, a letter — and spot a part that isn't quite right or could be better, all by themselves without you or a teacher pointing it out?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Short Research Projects
topics.description: Conduct short research projects that build knowledge about a topic, gather information from print and digital sources, and take brief organised notes
evidence: Generate three research questions about an assigned topic and identify two sources for each
Take brief notes from a print source, sorting key facts into provided categories
Write a short summary paragraph synthesising information gathered from two different sources
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is given a research project at school, can they look up information from books or websites, take organised notes, and then write it up in their own words?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Vivid Word Choices
topics.description: Choose precise and vivid words and phrases to create specific effects in writing
evidence: Replace vague words in 'The nice man went to the big house' with more precise alternatives and explain the effect
Write two versions of the same scene — one with plain language and one with carefully chosen words for suspense or humour
Select from a word bank the most effective verb and adjective for a given sentence, justifying each choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes descriptive or creative pieces, do they choose interesting and precise words — like "sprinted" instead of "ran", or "crimson" instead of "red" — to create a specific effect?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing Craft Vocabulary
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of writing craft and effect — form, structure, register, tone, voice, coherence, cohesion, argument, evidence, perspective, rhetoric, technique, formal, informal, and style — and understand that these words describe choices writers make intentionally to achieve a particular effect on the reader
evidence: Explain the difference between 'formal register' and 'informal register' and give an example of when each is appropriate
Use terms like 'coherence', 'cohesion', and 'paragraph structure' accurately when discussing or improving their own writing
Identify the 'purpose', 'audience', and 'form' of a piece of writing and explain how these shape the language choices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is writing a persuasive letter compared to a story, can they explain the difference in 'tone' and 'register' — and why they'd make different word choices for each one?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Choosing Form and Tone for Your Audience
topics.description: Identify the audience for and purpose of writing before beginning, selecting the appropriate form, tone, and register to match the intended reader and communicative goal
evidence: Determine the audience (e.g., peers, teacher, younger children, a public audience) and purpose (to persuade, inform, entertain, or explain) before drafting and explain how these choices affect language and structure
Select an appropriate form for the writing task (letter, report, story, instructions, review) based on audience and purpose
Adjust vocabulary, sentence length, and level of formality to suit the identified audience, e.g. using simpler language for younger readers and more formal language for an official letter
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} starts a piece of writing, do they think about who will read it and why — adjusting their tone, vocabulary, and format accordingly, like writing more formally for a teacher than for a friend?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Evidence-Based Writing
topics.description: Draw evidence from informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to non-fiction
evidence: Write a research-based paragraph or short report that cites specific facts, details, and evidence from informational texts to support key points
Synthesise information from two informational sources into a written summary that accurately represents both, noting areas of agreement and difference
Paraphrase information from informational texts accurately and cite sources appropriately, avoiding plagiarism
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a non-fiction piece — like a report on climate change — do they draw on specific facts and evidence from things they've read, weaving that information into their own writing?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Literary Evidence in Writing
topics.description: Draw evidence from literary texts to support analysis, reflection, and research in writing, applying grade-level reading standards to literature
evidence: Write a response to a literary text that includes direct quotations and specific details from the text as evidence to support a claim or observation
Explain how a character's actions or dialogue reveal their traits or motivations, citing specific passages from the story as evidence
Compare how two literary texts treat a similar theme, using textual evidence from both to support the comparison
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes about a book they've read — like an essay about a character or a theme — do they support their ideas with specific quotes or details drawn directly from the text?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing for an audience
topics.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organisation are appropriate to the task, purpose, and audience, maintaining a consistent style and structure throughout
evidence: Identify the task, purpose, and audience before writing and make deliberate choices about structure, tone, and vocabulary to suit them
Organise ideas logically so that the writing flows from introduction through development to conclusion, with each section serving a clear purpose
Review a draft to check that the organisation, style, and level of formality are consistent and appropriate for the intended reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes for school, does the piece feel well-organised and appropriate for its purpose — whether it's a formal essay, a creative story, or a persuasive argument — with a consistent tone throughout?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Layout and Formatting in Informational Writing
topics.description: Use layout devices including headings, sub-headings, columns, bullets, and tables to structure text and guide the reader through informational and explanatory writing
evidence: Organise an informational text using headings and sub-headings to separate sections
Present comparative information using a table with clear row and column headers
Use columns and bullet points to display information in a scannable format
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} writes a non-fiction piece — like a guide or an explanation — do they use layout features like headings, bullet points, and columns to help the reader navigate the information easily?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Planning Narratives
topics.description: Plan narrative writing by considering how authors have developed characters and settings, drawing on techniques observed in texts read, heard, or performed
evidence: Identify specific authorial techniques for character development from a mentor text
Plan a character using techniques such as showing through action borrowed from a studied author
Analyse how an author builds setting and apply similar techniques in planning own narrative
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} is about to write a story, do they think ahead about what their main character is like and where the story will take place before they start writing?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Research & Note-Taking
topics.description: Gather relevant information from print and digital sources, summarise or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a basic bibliography or list of sources
evidence: Take organised notes from multiple sources using own words rather than copying
Create a bibliography listing sources used in a research project
Paraphrase key information from a source without changing the meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is researching a topic for a school project, can they find information from books or websites, put it in their own words, and keep track of where they got it from?

topics.subject: English
topics.name: Writing a Précis
topics.description: Precis longer passages by summarising the main ideas and key information concisely while maintaining the essential meaning and removing non-essential detail
evidence: Reduce a three-paragraph text to a single paragraph capturing all main points
Identify and remove redundant information while preserving essential meaning
Write a precis that is no more than one-third the length of the original text
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a long article about a topic they're studying, can they write a short summary in their own words that captures the key points without copying sentences?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 10 using objects or drawings
evidence: Solve 'There are 6 apples, 2 are eaten, how many left?' using counters
Solve 'add to' and 'take from' result-unknown problems
Solve 'put together/take apart' problems with total unknown
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'There are 7 birds on a fence and 3 fly away — how many are left?', can {{name}} work it out using their fingers, counters, or a quick drawing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition as combining or putting together two
topics.description: Understand addition as combining or putting together two groups to find the total
evidence: Model 'putting together' with physical objects and say the total
Act out an 'add to' situation (e.g. 3 children arrive, then 2 more join)
Explain that addition means finding how many altogether
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 4 toy cars and a friend brings 3 more, do they understand that adding means combining both groups — and can they tell you there are now 7 cars altogether?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number bonds to 9
topics.description: Find the number that makes 10 when added to a given number from 1 to 9 (number bonds to 10)
evidence: Given 7, respond '3' to make 10
Use a ten-frame to find the complement to 10
Record pairs that make 10 as equations (e.g. 6 + 4 = 10)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and needs 10 for a recipe, can they quickly tell you they need 4 more — without counting all the way up from 1?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers up to 10 into pairs
topics.description: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way (part-part-whole)
evidence: Use objects or drawings to find all pairs that make a given number
Record decompositions as equations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 8 grapes, can they split them into two groups in different ways — like 3 and 5, or 4 and 4 — and explain that both groups together still make 8?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing Addition and Subtraction
topics.description: Represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, and mental images
evidence: Use cubes or counters to show 3 + 2
Draw a picture to represent a subtraction situation
Use fingers to model an addition problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 3 apples and you give them 2 more, can they show you how many there are altogether — using their fingers, some small objects, or a drawing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subtraction as taking away or separating
topics.description: Understand subtraction as taking away or separating from a group to find how many remain
evidence: Model 'taking away' with physical objects and say how many remain
Act out a 'take from' situation (e.g. 5 biscuits, eat 2, how many left?)
Explain that subtraction means finding how many are left
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 9 biscuits and eats 3, do they understand that subtracting means taking some away — and can they tell you 6 biscuits are left?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting
topics.description: Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero
evidence: Calculate 14 + 5 = 19
Calculate 17 – 3 = 14
Add or subtract 0 and explain the result stays the same
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '14 + 5' or '18 − 6' in their head or on paper, and do they know that adding or taking away zero leaves the number unchanged?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Early Word Problems
topics.description: Solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems
evidence: Solve 'I have 12 sweets and eat 4, how many left?'
Solve missing number: 7 = [ ] – 9
Solve problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'I had some sweets, ate 5, and now have 9 left — how many did I start with?', can {{name}} figure out the missing number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 5
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 5
evidence: Answer 2 + 3 quickly without counting on fingers
Answer 5 – 2 from recall or with minimal counting
Complete a set of within-5 addition/subtraction facts accurately and quickly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} give you the answer to sums like '2 + 3' or '5 − 2' straight away, without needing to count on their fingers every time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number bonds
topics.description: Recall number bonds (addition and related subtraction facts) within 20
evidence: Quickly recall that 8 + 5 = 13
Given 13 – 5, respond 8 using knowledge of related addition fact
Know all pairs of single-digit numbers that sum to numbers up to 20
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '8 + 7 = 15' and immediately know that '15 − 7 = 8' — without having to work out the subtraction from scratch?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading +, −, and = symbols
topics.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols +, −, and = in number sentences
evidence: Read 3 + 2 = 5 aloud as 'three plus two equals five'
Write a number sentence to match a concrete addition situation
Interpret the = sign as 'is the same as' rather than just 'the answer is'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you write '4 + 3 = 7' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the plus sign, minus sign, and equals sign each mean?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting tens mentally
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 45 + 30 = 75 mentally
Calculate 82 − 40 = 42 mentally
Explain that only the tens digit changes when adding/subtracting tens
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '54 + 30' or '78 − 20' in their head — knowing that only the tens digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Three Small Numbers
topics.description: Add three one-digit numbers using strategies including looking for pairs that make 10
evidence: Calculate 5 + 7 + 3 by first adding 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15
Add any three single-digit numbers correctly
Identify useful pairs within three addends to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 4 + 6 + 8, can they spot that 4 and 6 make 10 first, then add 8 to get 18 — rather than just adding in order from left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding two two-digit numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mental methods
evidence: Calculate 34 + 27 using base-ten blocks or column addition
Calculate 63 − 28 using a number line or partitioning
Explain a strategy for adding or subtracting two two-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract two two-digit numbers — like '43 + 28' — using counters, a drawing, or working it out in their head?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding within 100
topics.description: Add within 100 using strategies based on place value, including adding a two-digit and one-digit number, and a two-digit and a multiple of 10
evidence: Calculate 46 + 7 using place value (46 + 4 + 3 = 53)
Calculate 38 + 40 = 78 using tens understanding
Relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '47 + 8' or '35 + 50' by thinking about the tens and ones separately rather than counting up one at a time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
topics.description: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction
evidence: Add 8 + 3 by starting at 8 and counting on 3 (9, 10, 11)
Subtract 12 − 3 by counting back 3 from 12 (11, 10, 9)
Explain that counting on is a way to add
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 5', can they start from 8 and count up five more — rather than starting from 1 every time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 20
topics.description: Add and subtract within 20 using strategies such as making ten, decomposing a number leading to ten, and using known facts
evidence: Solve 8 + 6 using making ten: 8 + 2 + 4 = 14
Solve 13 − 4 by decomposing: 13 − 3 − 1 = 9
Use a known fact (8 + 4 = 12) to derive 12 − 8 = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 6', can they split the 6 into 2 + 4, use the 2 to fill up to 10, then add the remaining 4 to get 14?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition in any order
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order
evidence: Explain that 3 + 8 gives the same answer as 8 + 3
Use commutativity to choose the larger number to count on from
Demonstrate that subtraction is not commutative (5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 6 + 4 gives the same answer as 4 + 6, so they can always choose whichever order makes the adding easier?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding a missing number in addition
topics.description: Understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend (e.g. 10 − 8 = ? is the same as 8 + ? = 10)
evidence: Solve 10 − 8 by thinking 'what do I add to 8 to make 10?'
Explain that subtraction can be thought of as a missing-addend problem
Use known addition facts to solve related subtraction problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} see that '10 − 8 = ?' is the same as asking 'what do I add to 8 to reach 10?' — so they can use their adding knowledge to help with subtraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 10
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 10
evidence: Answer any addition fact within 10 quickly from memory
Answer any subtraction fact within 10 quickly from memory
Complete a timed set of within-10 facts with high accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer sums like '7 + 3' or '9 − 4' almost instantly — without stopping to count on their fingers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction
topics.description: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
evidence: Rapidly recall 7 + 8 = 15 and 15 − 8 = 7
Use 6 + 4 = 10 to derive 60 + 40 = 100
Derive 35 + 5 = 40 from knowledge that 5 + 5 = 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '9 + 7 = 16' and '16 − 7 = 9', and use those to help work out bigger sums like '90 + 70'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Grouping numbers to add
topics.description: Understand and apply the associative property of addition: when adding three numbers, any two can be added first
evidence: Solve 2 + 6 + 4 by first adding 6 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 10 = 12
Explain that grouping addends differently gives the same total
Choose which two numbers to add first to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3 + 7 + 6, can they spot that adding 3 and 7 first (to make 10) is easier — rather than always working left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Inverse: addition undoes subtraction
topics.description: Recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems
evidence: Check 15 + 7 = 22 by calculating 22 − 7 = 15
Use the inverse to solve: □ + 9 = 14, so □ = 14 − 9 = 5
Explain that addition and subtraction 'undo' each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out 13 + 5 = 18, can they immediately use that to say '18 − 5 = 13' — without having to work the subtraction out all over again?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 6+)
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 36 + 7 = 43 using objects or mentally
Calculate 52 − 4 = 48 using a number line or mentally
Explain bridging through 10 when adding ones to a two-digit number
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '36 + 7' or '42 − 5' in their head — keeping the tens in place and only adjusting the ones?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental and written addition and subtraction
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems using mental and written methods, including problems involving numbers, quantities, and measures
evidence: Solve a two-step problem: 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p. How much now?'
Choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for a given problem
Solve problems involving measures, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a problem involving lengths, weights, or prices, can they decide whether to add or subtract and carry out the calculation correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subtracting multiples of 10
topics.description: Subtract multiples of 10 (10–90) from multiples of 10 using place value strategies
evidence: Calculate 70 − 30 = 40
Use base-ten blocks to show 80 − 50 = 30
Explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '80 − 50' or '70 − 40' in their head by thinking about how many tens are left?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unknown in Addition & Subtraction
topics.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers
evidence: Solve 8 + ? = 11 and write 3
Solve 5 = □ − 3 and write 8
Solve 6 + 6 = □ and write 12

topics.name: Picture & Bar Graphs
topics.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories; solve put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Draw a picture graph with a symbol representing one unit for each data point
Draw a bar graph with labelled axes and a single-unit scale
Use a bar graph to answer comparison questions (e.g. 'How many more votes did cats get than dogs?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a simple bar chart or picture graph to show information — like how many of each colour of sweet are in a bag — and answer questions from it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar graphs
topics.description: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
evidence: Read a time graph showing temperature changes over a day
Present data about plant growth over weeks as a time graph
Explain the difference between a bar chart (discrete) and a time graph (continuous)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} choose the right type of chart for some data — for example, a bar chart for favourite colours or a line graph for temperature over a week — and draw it correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Representing numbers with objects (age 8+)
topics.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set; solve one- and two-step comparison, sum, and difference problems using bar charts, pictograms, and tables
evidence: Draw a bar graph where each square represents 5 pets
From a scaled pictogram, answer: how many more children chose football than tennis?
Solve a two-step problem: how many votes in total for the top two choices?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a bar chart showing how many books different children read last month, could they work out the total, find the difference between the most and least, and draw their own chart with a scale like "each square = 2 books"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and Comparing Bar Graphs
topics.description: Solve comparison, sum, and difference problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Read a line graph of temperature over a week and identify the warmest day
Find the difference in rainfall between two months from a line graph
Explain what a rising/falling line means on a time-series graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a line graph showing how a plant's height changed over several weeks, can they read off values, spot when it grew fastest, and find the difference between two points?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Complete, read, and interpret information in tables, including timetables
evidence: Read a bus timetable to find the departure time for a particular stop
Complete a two-way table from given data about favourite sports by gender
Calculate how long a train journey takes using a timetable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a timetable — like a train or bus timetable — to find out when a journey leaves, arrives, and how long it takes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical Analysis Vocabulary
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, range, frequency, data, sample, average, chart, table, graph, pie chart, scatter graph, correlation — with understanding of what each term describes
evidence: Correctly define and calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a small data set
Use 'outlier' correctly to identify a value that doesn't fit the pattern, and explain its effect on the mean
Use 'correlation' correctly when describing the relationship shown in a scatter graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a set of test scores from their class, could they find the mean, the median, and the range — and explain what each one tells you about how the class did?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating the Mean
topics.description: Calculate and interpret the mean as an average of a data set
evidence: Calculate the mean of five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95
Explain what the mean represents and how it differs from individual data values
Find a missing data value given the mean and all other values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the family scored 6, 8, 7, 5, and 9 on a board game over five rounds, can {{name}} work out the mean (average) score?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graphs (age 10+)
topics.description: Interpret and construct pie charts and line graphs; use these to solve problems
evidence: Read values from a line graph showing temperature over a day and identify trends
Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a pie chart — for example, one showing how a family spends its weekly budget — and use it to answer questions and solve problems?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); use operations on fractions to solve problems involving data in line plots (e.g. redistribute total equally)
evidence: Create a line plot showing lengths measured to the nearest 1/8 inch
Use the line plot to find the total of all measurements by adding fractions
Solve: 'If the total liquid were redistributed equally among all beakers, how much would each have?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the lengths of several objects to the nearest quarter or eighth of an inch and plotted them on a number line, could they use those measurements to work out totals or share amounts equally?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding halves and quarters (age 5+)
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into four equal parts and identify each as 'a quarter'
Find a quarter of 12 objects by sharing into 4 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into quarters (four equal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you fold a square piece of paper into four equal parts, can {{name}} tell you that each part is a quarter — and point to just one quarter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Is a Half?
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into two equal parts and identify each as 'a half'
Find half of 8 objects by sharing into 2 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into halves or not (equal vs unequal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is helping share a sandwich equally between two people, can they cut it so both pieces are the same size — and tell you each piece is called a half?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decomposing a shape into more equal shares
topics.description: Understand that decomposing a shape into more equal shares creates smaller shares
evidence: Explain that a quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza
Demonstrate that fourths are smaller pieces than halves
Compare the size of halves and quarters of the same shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pizza is shared between 2 people and then the same pizza is shared between 8 people, can {{name}} explain why each slice is smaller when more people share it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use fraction notation correctly — fraction, numerator, denominator, unit fraction, non-unit fraction, proper fraction, improper fraction, mixed number, equivalent fraction, simplest form — and understand what each term describes, including the roles of the numerator and denominator in expressing parts of a whole
evidence: Point to and name the numerator and denominator in any given fraction and explain what each tells you
Correctly classify fractions as unit, proper, improper, or mixed number with an example of each
Explain in own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent fractions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw the fraction 3/4 written down, could they point to the numerator and the denominator — and explain what each number actually means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts
topics.description: Recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
evidence: Find 1/3 of 12 objects by sharing into 3 equal groups
Shade 3/4 of a rectangle that has been divided into 4 equal parts
Identify 1/4 of a length on a number line or ruler
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you put 12 grapes on the table, can {{name}} count out a quarter of them — and then show you what three-quarters of the grapes looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves & Quarters of Shapes
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describe them using the words halves, fourths, and quarters
evidence: Divide a circle into two equal halves
Divide a rectangle into four equal quarters
Describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round pizza or a rectangular chocolate bar, can they divide it into four equal pieces and tell you each piece is called a quarter or a fourth?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
evidence: Write 1/2 of 10 = 5
Explain that 2/4 is the same as 1/2 using a diagram
Calculate simple unit fractions of quantities and write the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and eats half of them, can they write that as "1/2 of 6 = 3" — and explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions
topics.description: Compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominator
evidence: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest
Explain that a larger denominator means smaller unit fractions
Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and explain that 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 3/8 of a cake and a friend has eaten 5/8 of the same cake, can they tell you who has eaten more — and put those fractions in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving counting in tenths, fractions of quantities, equivalence, fraction addition/subtraction, and fraction comparison
evidence: Solve a word problem requiring finding a fraction of a quantity
Solve a problem that requires comparing or ordering fractions
Choose and apply appropriate fraction knowledge to a multi-step problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bag of 20 sweets is shared equally among 5 friends, can {{name}} work out what fraction each person gets — and how many sweets that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions
topics.description: Recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
evidence: Show that 1/2 = 2/4 using a diagram of equal parts
Use a fraction wall or bar model to find equivalent fractions
Explain why two fractions are equivalent by comparing the shaded areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a bar divided into 4 equal parts with 2 shaded, can they tell you that's the same as 1/2 — and draw a different bar showing the same amount another way?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Recognise and use fractions as numbers: place unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators on a number line
evidence: Place 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1
Identify that 1/3 lies between 0 and 1/2 on the number line
Understand that a fraction is a single number, not just 'part of a shape'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you draw a number line from 0 to 1, can {{name}} mark where 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 should go — without any extra help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple Fraction Sums
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7)
evidence: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5
Calculate 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8
Explain that when denominators are the same, you add/subtract the numerators
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 2/8 of a cup of milk and then another 3/8 of a cup, can {{name}} work out the total without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Splitting shapes into equal parts (age 7+)
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares; describe shares as halves, thirds, and fourths; recognise that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape
evidence: Partition a circle into 3 equal parts and label each 'a third'
Partition a rectangle into 4 equal shares in more than one way
Explain that two different-looking shares can still be equal in size
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a rectangle into thirds in two different ways (three strips vs three squares), can {{name}} recognise that both give equal thirds — even though the pieces look different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths
topics.description: Count up and down in tenths; recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and from dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10
evidence: Count: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths … up to ten tenths (one whole)
Show that dividing a shape into 10 equal parts gives tenths
Explain that 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} splits a chocolate bar with 10 equal pieces, can they tell you each piece is one tenth — and count up from 1/10 to 10/10 in order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unit fractions
topics.description: Recognise, find, and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
evidence: Find 1/4 of 12 objects by dividing into 4 equal groups
Find 3/4 of 12 objects
Write the fraction of a set that is shaded or selected
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 books on a shelf, can {{name}} work out how many two-thirds of them is — and check by grouping the books into three equal piles?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, including results greater than one whole (e.g. 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8)
evidence: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 and explain it equals 1 2/5
Subtract 2/6 from 5/6
Solve addition problems where the sum exceeds the whole: 7/8 + 3/8
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 5/8 of a bag of flour and then another 6/8, can {{name}} work out the total and explain what the answer means as a mixed number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about size; record comparisons with >, =, or < symbols
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 3/4: same numerator, larger denominator means smaller pieces so 3/8 < 3/4
Compare 5/6 and 2/6: same denominator so 5/6 > 2/6
Justify a comparison using a visual model and explain why both fractions must refer to the same whole
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/5 and 3/8, can they tell you which is bigger just by thinking about the size of each piece — without needing to draw it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths
topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of any number of tenths or hundredths (e.g. 3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27)
evidence: Write 7/10 as 0.7 and vice versa
Convert 45/100 to 0.45
Place 0.3 and 3/10 at the same point on a number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 7/10 on a price label, can they rewrite it as a decimal — and do the same thing for 43/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal & Percent Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use decimal and percentage notation correctly — decimal, decimal point, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, percentage, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and understand the relationships between fractions, decimals, and percentages as three ways of expressing the same value
evidence: Read and write decimal numbers correctly, identifying the value of each digit (ones, tenths, hundredths)
Use the % symbol correctly and explain that per cent means 'out of 100'
Convert between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages (e.g. 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) and explain why they are equal
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw '0.5' and '50%' written down, could they explain that they both mean the same amount — and write them as a fraction too?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Round decimals with one decimal place to the nearest whole number
evidence: Round 3.7 to 4 and 3.2 to 3
Place 6.5 on a number line between 6 and 7 and decide it rounds to 7
Round a set of one-decimal-place numbers and explain the rounding rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures something as 3.7 m, can they tell you whether that rounds to 3 m or 4 m — and explain why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare numbers with the same number of decimal places up to two decimal places
evidence: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest
Compare 3.72 and 3.27 using place-value reasoning
Place three two-decimal-place numbers on a number line in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing two prices — £4.75 and £4.57 — can they tell you which is more expensive without using a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions
topics.description: Solve simple measure and money problems involving fractions and decimals to two decimal places
evidence: Calculate 1/4 of £3.20
A rope is 2.5 m long; how much is left after cutting 0.75 m?
Find 3/10 of 1 kg and express the answer in grams and as a decimal of a kg
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bottle holds 1.5 litres and {{name}} drinks 0.75 litres, can they work out how much is left — and write it as both a decimal and a fraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by 10 and 100
topics.description: Find the effect of dividing a one- or two-digit number by 10 and 100, identifying the value of the digits as ones, tenths, and hundredths
evidence: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and identify 3 as ones and 7 as tenths
Calculate 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 and identify 4 as hundredths
Explain that dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts with the number 48 and divides it by 10, can they tell you the answer — and explain what happened to each digit's place value?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate simple equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent using visual fraction models
evidence: Given 1/3, generate 2/6 as equivalent and show with area model
Simplify 4/8 to 1/2 and justify with a fraction strip
Complete equivalence chains: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a fraction bar split into 3 parts with 1 shaded (= 1/3), can they draw an equivalent bar with 6 parts that shows exactly the same amount shaded?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions on a number line
topics.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size or the same point on a number line; recognise and show families of common equivalent fractions using diagrams
evidence: Use fraction strips to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6
Verify on a number line that 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point
Identify at least three fractions equivalent to 1/2 using diagrams
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same point on a number line, can they explain in their own words why those two fractions are equal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction-Decimal Equivalents
topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4
evidence: Match fractions to decimals in a sorting activity
Explain why 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 using a hundredths grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 3/4 of a cup of flour, can {{name}} tell you what that is as a decimal — without looking it up?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions as parts of shapes
topics.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole
evidence: Partition a rectangle into 6 equal-area parts and label each 1/6
Show two different ways to partition a square into 4 equal parts
Given a pre-partitioned shape, write the unit fraction for one part
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to fold a square piece of paper into 8 equal parts, can they tell you what fraction of the whole square each part represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts (harder)
topics.description: Solve problems involving increasingly harder fractions to calculate quantities, including non-unit fractions where the answer is a whole number
evidence: Find 3/5 of 20
Calculate 2/3 of 18 and explain the two-step process (divide then multiply)
Solve: A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red — how many red sweets?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If 3/4 of a class of 28 pupils brought their homework in, can {{name}} work out exactly how many pupils that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole
topics.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a/b as a parts of size 1/b
evidence: Given a shape divided into 5 equal parts, identify one shaded part as 1/5
Explain that 3/4 means 3 parts each of size 1/4
Draw a model showing 2/6 as 2 pieces of a whole cut into 6
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a pizza into 6 equal slices, can {{name}} explain what 1/6 means — and then work out what 4/6 of the pizza looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 8+)
topics.description: Express whole numbers as fractions (e.g. 3 = 3/1) and recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers (e.g. 4/4 = 1, 6/1 = 6)
evidence: Write 5 as 5/1 and explain why
Locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point on a number line
Identify which fractions from a list equal a whole number: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to write the number 3 as a fraction, can they write 3/1 — and also tell you what fraction equals exactly 1 whole, like 4/4 or 5/5?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line (age 8+)
topics.description: Represent fractions on a number line: partition the interval 0 to 1 into b equal parts to locate 1/b, then mark off a lengths of 1/b from 0 to locate a/b
evidence: Partition a 0-to-1 number line into 4 equal parts and mark 1/4
Explain that each part on the line has size 1/b
Locate 1/3 and 1/6 on separate number lines
Locate 3/4 on a number line by counting three 1/4-jumps from 0
Place 5/6 on a number line and explain the process
Identify a fraction shown by a point on a pre-partitioned number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a number line from 0 to 1 split into 5 equal parts, can they label where 2/5 and 4/5 go — and explain how they worked it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths (age 8+)
topics.description: Count up and down in hundredths; recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by 100 or dividing tenths by 10
evidence: Count from 3/100 to 12/100 in hundredths
Explain that 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100
Place several hundredths on a number line between 0 and 1/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has £1 and spends 37p, can they say that 37p is 37/100 of a pound — and count up in hundredths from 0/100 to 100/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, including by converting to improper fractions or using properties of operations
evidence: Calculate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 and express as a mixed number
Subtract 3 1/4 from 5 3/4
Solve 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 by regrouping the whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 1 and 2/5 cups of oats and another batch needs 2 and 3/5 cups, can {{name}} add them together to get the total — including converting when the fifths add up past a whole?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding fractions (different denominators)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with denominators that are multiples of the same number by finding a common denominator
evidence: Calculate 1/3 + 1/6 by converting to sixths: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
Calculate 3/4 − 1/8 by converting to eighths
Add 2/5 + 3/10 and simplify the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 1/3 and 1/6, can they find a common denominator and work out the total — showing their working?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators, using visual models and equations
evidence: A jug contains 3/4 litre of juice; 2/4 litre is poured out — how much remains?
Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/8 and 1 5/8 inches — what is their total length?
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a fraction word problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that one section of a nature trail is 3/8 km and another is 5/8 km, can they work out the total distance without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Decimals
topics.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths (or up to three decimal places) by reasoning about size using place-value understanding; record with >, =, <
evidence: Compare 0.45 and 0.405 and explain which is greater
Order 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 from smallest to largest
Justify that 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 using place-value reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares 0.45 and 0.54, can they use place value to explain which is bigger — without reaching for a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Compare and order fractions with different numerators and denominators by creating common denominators/numerators or comparing to a benchmark such as 1/2; justify conclusions with visual models
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 5/12 by finding a common denominator of 24
Order 2/3, 3/5, and 7/10 from smallest to largest
Use the benchmark 1/2 to decide that 5/8 > 3/7
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 2/3 of their lunch and a friend has eaten 3/4 of theirs, can they work out who's eaten more — by finding a common way to compare the fractions?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting tenths to hundredths
topics.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100 and use this to add fractions with denominators 10 and 100 (e.g. 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100)
evidence: Rewrite 7/10 as 70/100
Explain why 5/10 = 50/100 using a hundredths grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3/10 and 17/100, can they rewrite 3/10 as hundredths first — and then add the two fractions together?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value (age 9+)
topics.description: Round decimals with two decimal places to the nearest whole number and to one decimal place
evidence: Round 3.47 to the nearest whole number (3) and to 1 d.p. (3.5)
Round 12.95 to 1 d.p. (13.0) and explain the boundary case
Estimate 4.83 + 2.17 by rounding each to the nearest whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a length as 4.67 m, can they round it to the nearest whole metre — and also to the nearest tenth of a metre?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals for Tenths & Hundredths
topics.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100; read and write decimal numbers as fractions (e.g. 0.62 = 62/100, 0.71 = 71/100)
evidence: Rewrite 0.62 as 62/100
Write 3/10 as 0.3 and locate on a number line
Read 0.07 and express as 7/100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a price tag showing £0.65, can they rewrite it as a fraction — and go the other way, turning 47/100 into a decimal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals to three places
topics.description: Solve problems involving numbers with up to three decimal places
evidence: Calculate the total of three measurements: 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m
A bottle holds 1.5 litres; 0.375 l is poured out — how much remains?
Find two numbers with 3 d.p. that add to make 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a tank that holds 5.000 litres and has poured in 2.375 litres, can they work out how much more is needed to fill it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to (n×a)/(n×b) using visual models; use this principle to recognise and generate equivalent fractions, including tenths and hundredths
evidence: Use a fraction strip to show 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9
Explain that multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction because the size of the whole is unchanged
Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify with diagrams
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make 2/3 look different without changing its value, can they multiply the top and bottom by the same number and explain why the fraction stays the same?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Addition Concepts
topics.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts; decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way
evidence: Write two different decompositions of 5/6
Use a visual model to justify a decomposition of 2 1/8 into whole-number and fraction parts
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 7/8 of a chocolate bar and gives away 3/8, can they work out what fraction is left — and then show two different ways to split 7/8 into two parts?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number using visual models and equations
evidence: Each person eats 3/8 of a pizza and there are 5 people — how many pizzas are needed?
A ribbon is cut into pieces of 2/3 metre; how long are 4 pieces altogether?
Between what two whole numbers does 6 × 3/4 lie?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If each section of a garden uses 3/4 of a bag of compost and there are 4 sections, can {{name}} work out how many bags are needed in total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
topics.description: Recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions; convert from one form to the other (e.g. 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
evidence: Convert 11/4 to 2 3/4
Convert 3 2/5 to 17/5
Write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 = 2 as both improper fraction and whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the fraction 9/4, can they convert it to a mixed number — and then turn 2 and 3/5 back into an improper fraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying fractions
topics.description: Understand a/b as a multiple of 1/b; multiply proper fractions and mixed numbers by whole numbers, supported by visual models (e.g. 3 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5)
evidence: Calculate 4 × 3/8 using repeated addition or the rule n × a/b = (n×a)/b
Multiply 2 1/3 × 3 and express as a mixed number
Use a visual model to show why 5 × 1/4 = 5/4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of butter and {{name}} wants to make it three times over, can they work out how much butter they need in total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentage and decimal equivalents
topics.description: Solve problems requiring knowledge of percentage and decimal equivalents of 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and fractions with denominators that are multiples of 10 or 25
evidence: State that 1/5 = 20% = 0.2 and use this to find 20% of 60
Convert 3/4 to 75% and to 0.75
A shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that 1/4 = 25% = 0.25, can they use that to work out 25% of £80 — and also find 4/5 of 60 sweets?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths (age 9+)
topics.description: Recognise and use thousandths; relate them to tenths, hundredths, and their decimal equivalents (e.g. 1/1000 = 0.001, 35/1000 = 0.035)
evidence: Explain that 1 tenth = 100 thousandths
Place 0.345 on a number line between 0.34 and 0.35
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the decimal 0.003, can they write it as a fraction and tell you roughly where it sits on a number line between 0 and 0.01?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions (age 9+)
topics.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b (e.g. 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5)
evidence: Express 5/8 as a sum of five copies of 1/8
Show on a number line how 4/3 is built by iterating 1/3 four times
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to show 4/5 as a sum of smaller equal fractions, can they write it out as 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding Percentages
topics.description: Understand the per cent symbol (%); know that per cent means ‘number of parts per hundred’; write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal
evidence: Write 35% as 35/100 and as 0.35
Shade 40% of a 10×10 grid and write the fraction 40/100
Explain that 100% means the whole, 50% means half
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a shop advertises 50% off, can {{name}} explain that this means half price — and write 50% as both a fraction and a decimal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Fractions (Unlike Denominators)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions to produce a common denominator
evidence: Compute 2/3 + 5/4 by converting to twelfths: 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12
Subtract 1 3/5 from 3 1/4 using a common denominator
Explain the strategy of finding a common denominator and verify using a visual model
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 2/3 of a cup of one ingredient and 3/4 of another, can {{name}} add those fractions together — even though the denominators are different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area with Fractions
topics.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling with unit-fraction squares; show that the area equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 2/3 × 3/4 rectangle with 1/12 squares and count to find area = 6/12 = 1/2
Explain why the number of unit-fraction tiles equals the product of the two fractions
Calculate the area of a rectangle with sides 1 1/2 and 2/3 using fraction multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a piece of fabric is 2/3 m long and 3/4 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area — and explain how tiling it with tiny fraction-squares shows the same answer as multiplying?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Compare and order fractions including fractions greater than 1, by converting to common denominators or using benchmarks
evidence: Order 3/4, 7/8, 5/6, and 11/12 from smallest to largest
Compare 7/5 and 4/3 using common denominators
Place improper fractions and mixed numbers on a number line in correct order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to sort 5/3, 7/4, and 2/1 in order from smallest to biggest, can they convert them to a common denominator and order them correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions (age 10+)
topics.description: Associate a fraction with division and calculate decimal fraction equivalents for simple fractions (e.g. 3/8 = 0.375); recall and use equivalences between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages in different contexts
evidence: Convert 3/8 to 0.375 by dividing 3 ÷ 8
State that 1/5 = 0.2 = 20% from memory
Use fraction–decimal–percentage equivalences to compare 30%, 1/3, and 0.35 and put them in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/8 written on a worksheet, can they convert it to a decimal — and also say roughly what percentage that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by Fractions
topics.description: Interpret and compute division of a whole number by a unit fraction (e.g. 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain why the quotient is larger than the dividend
evidence: Compute 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 and explain: 'How many fifths fit in 4 wholes?'
Create a story context for 6 ÷ (1/4) and solve it
Verify 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 by showing 20 × (1/5) = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you have 4 metres of ribbon and each bow needs 1/5 of a metre, can {{name}} work out how many bows you can make — and explain why the answer is bigger than 4?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing fractions (unit fractions)
topics.description: Interpret and compute division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number (e.g. 1/3 ÷ 4 = 1/12); use visual models and the relationship between multiplication and division to explain the result
evidence: Compute (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 and explain using a visual model of splitting 1/3 into 4 equal parts
Create a story context for (1/6) ÷ 3 and solve it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 1/3 of a bag of rice and splits it into 4 equal portions, can they work out what fraction of the whole bag each portion is — and explain why the answer is smaller than 1/3?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing unit fractions and whole numbers
topics.description: Solve real-world problems involving division of unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions, using visual models and equations
evidence: Solve: '3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally — how much each?' (1/6 lb)
Solve: 'How many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups of raisins?' (6 servings)
Create a story context for a given unit-fraction division expression
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has half a pizza to share equally among 3 people, can they work out what fraction of the whole pizza each person gets — and explain the steps they took?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 10+)
