topics.description: Recognise and use language relating to dates, including days of the week, weeks, months, and years
evidence: Name the seven days of the week in order
Name the twelve months of the year in order
Understand that a year is made up of months and weeks
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} what day it is today, what day yesterday was, and what month we're in, can they answer all three — and tell you how many months are in a year?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length and height (age 5+)
topics.description: Measure and begin to record lengths and heights using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Measure the length of a table using cubes and record the result
Begin to use a ruler to measure in centimetres
Record a measurement as a number with a unit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the length of a book using small cubes laid end to end, can they count how many cubes it takes — and then try measuring the same book with a ruler?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring mass and weight
topics.description: Measure and begin to record mass/weight using non-standard and standard units
evidence: Use a balance to compare masses of two objects
Measure mass using non-standard units (e.g. 'this book weighs 5 cubes')
Begin to read a simple scale for mass
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses balance scales to compare two objects, can they tell you which is heavier — and if given weights like 100g, can they balance an object on the scale?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling Time: Hours and Half Hours
topics.description: Tell the time to the hour and half past the hour, and draw clock hands to show these times
evidence: Read an analogue clock showing 3 o'clock
Read an analogue clock showing half past 7
Draw the hour and minute hands on a blank clock face to show a given o'clock or half-past time
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you point to a clock showing 3 o'clock or half past two, can {{name}} tell you the time — and then draw hands on a blank clock face to show a time you call out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to the minute
topics.description: Measure and begin to record time in hours, minutes, and seconds
evidence: Use a sand timer or stopwatch to time an activity
Begin to understand that 1 minute = 60 seconds
Record a duration in simple terms (e.g. 'it took about 2 minutes')
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} watches the second hand go all the way round a clock, can they count that as one minute — and estimate roughly how many minutes their favourite TV show lasts?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding money and giving change
topics.description: Find different combinations of coins that equal the same amount of money
evidence: Show that 50p can be made with 2×20p + 1×10p, or 5×10p, or 1×50p
Systematically find multiple coin combinations for a given total
Explain why different coin sets give the same total
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to make exactly 30p, can they find two or three different ways to do it using different combinations of coins?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing measurement units
topics.description: Choose and use appropriate standard units to measure length (m/cm), mass (kg/g), temperature (°C), and capacity (litres/ml) to the nearest appropriate unit
evidence: Measure the length of a table in centimetres using a ruler
Weigh an object in grams using a scale
Measure the capacity of a container in millilitres using a measuring jug
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} whether to measure a swimming pool or a piece of paper in cm or m, can they pick the sensible unit for each — and explain why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing and ordering measurements
topics.description: Compare and order lengths, mass, and capacity and record results using >, <, and =
evidence: Measure two objects and write 45cm > 32cm
Order three containers by capacity after measuring each
Use = when two measurements are the same
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures three pieces of string as 15 cm, 9 cm, and 22 cm, can they put them in order from shortest to longest — and write that using a < symbol?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length
topics.description: Order three objects by length and compare the lengths of two objects indirectly using a third object
evidence: Put three ribbons in order from shortest to longest
Use a piece of string to compare the heights of two objects that cannot be placed side by side
Explain that if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has three pencils of different lengths but can only compare two at a time, can they figure out which is longest — by using a third pencil as a go-between?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 6+)
topics.description: Measure the length of an object using same-size length units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
evidence: Measure a book by laying paper clips end to end and counting them
Understand that the length measurement is the number of units that span the object
Avoid gaps and overlaps when placing units
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is measuring the length of a table using identical toy bricks, can they lay them end to end with no gaps — and tell you how many bricks long the table is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money Addition & Subtraction
topics.description: Solve simple money problems involving addition and subtraction, including giving change
evidence: Calculate the total cost of two items priced in pence
Work out change from 50p after buying an item costing 35p
Solve 'How much more money do I need?' problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} buys a snack for 45p and pays with a £1 coin, can they work out how much change they should get — and count it back?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number of minutes in an hour
topics.description: Know the number of minutes in an hour and the number of hours in a day
evidence: State that there are 60 minutes in an hour
State that there are 24 hours in a day
Use these facts to solve simple time problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows there are 60 minutes in an hour, can they tell you how many minutes are in 2 hours — and how many hours make a whole day?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pounds & Pence Notation
topics.description: Recognise and use symbols for pounds (£) and pence (p) and combine amounts to make a particular value
evidence: Write £1.50 or 150p correctly
Combine coins to make a given total, e.g. 50p + 20p + 5p = 75p
Read prices written with £ and p symbols
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} picks up coins worth 50p, 20p, and 10p, can they write the total using the p symbol — and tell you if that's enough to buy something costing 75p?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sequence intervals of time
topics.description: Compare and sequence intervals of time
evidence: Order three events by how long they took
Compare the duration of two activities (e.g. 'the race took longer than the walk')
Sequence intervals on a timeline
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows a film takes 2 hours and a car journey takes 45 minutes, can they tell you which takes longer — and put a few daily activities in order of how long they take?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling Time: Minutes
topics.description: Tell and write the time to five minutes, including quarter past and quarter to, and draw clock hands to show these times
evidence: Read an analogue clock showing 3:25
Write 'quarter past 9' or '9:15'
Draw clock hands to show twenty to four
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the clock shows quarter to four, can {{name}} tell you the time — and draw hands on a blank clock face to show twenty past three?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving lengths within 100, using addition and subtraction with drawings and equations
evidence: Solve 'The rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a diagram (e.g. a ruler drawing) to represent a length word problem
Write an equation with a symbol for the unknown to represent the problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a piece of rope 75 cm long and cuts off 28 cm, can they work out how much rope is left — and draw a number-line diagram to show it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating with measurements
topics.description: Measure, compare, add, and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g), and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units
evidence: Measure a length in centimetres and millimetres
Weigh an object using grams and kilograms
Add two measurements in the same unit (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pours 350 ml into a jug and then adds another 275 ml, can they work out the total — and tell you how much more is needed to reach 1 litre?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing lengths by measuring
topics.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit
evidence: Measure two objects and calculate the difference in length
Express the difference using the correct unit (e.g. '7 cm longer')
Solve a comparison problem: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pencil is 16 cm and a crayon is 9 cm, can {{name}} work out how much longer the pencil is — without measuring them side by side?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Time Durations
topics.description: Compare durations of events and calculate the time taken by particular events or tasks
evidence: Calculate how long an activity lasted given start and end times
Compare the duration of two events and identify which was longer
Solve a problem such as 'The lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00. How long is it?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts cooking at 4:15 p.m. and finishes at 5:00 p.m., can they work out how long the cooking took?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating answers (age 7+)
topics.description: Estimate and read time with increasing accuracy to the nearest minute; record and compare time in terms of seconds, minutes, and hours
evidence: Read an analogue clock to the nearest minute
Estimate how long an activity takes in minutes or seconds
Compare two durations and determine which is longer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a TV show starts at 5:17 p.m. and ends at 5:43 p.m., can {{name}} work out how long it lasted — and express that in minutes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating Lengths
topics.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimetres, and metres
evidence: Estimate the length of a classroom object before measuring it
Use a known reference (e.g. width of a finger ≈ 1 cm) to make reasonable estimates
Check estimates by measuring and evaluate how close they were
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a car parked outside, can they estimate roughly how many metres long it is — and then check whether their guess was reasonable?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Giving Change
topics.description: Add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts
evidence: Calculate the total cost of two or three items priced in pounds and pence
Work out the change from £5 or £10
Record money calculations using £ and p notation correctly (e.g. £3.47)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} buys a book for £3.50 and a pencil for £1.25 with a £5 note, can they work out exactly how much change they should receive?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves and quarters (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately
evidence: Determine the total value of a collection of coins
Solve a word problem about making change with US currency
Use $ and ¢ symbols correctly in answers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 2 quarters, 1 dime, and 3 pennies, can they work out the total — and tell you whether that's enough to buy something costing 65 cents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 7+)
topics.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, metre sticks, and measuring tapes
evidence: Choose the most appropriate tool for measuring a given object
Align the zero mark of a ruler with the end of the object and read the measurement
Measure lengths in inches, feet, centimetres, and metres using the correct tool
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to measure a piece of fabric about 80 cm long, can they pick the right tool — a short ruler or a tape measure — and use it accurately?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Perimeters
topics.description: Measure the perimeter of simple 2-D shapes
evidence: Measure each side of a rectangle and add the lengths to find the perimeter
Calculate the perimeter of a regular shape given the side length
Explain that perimeter is the total distance around a shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to put a decorative border around a rectangular picture frame 20 cm wide and 30 cm tall, can they work out the total length of border needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring & Plotting Lengths
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest whole unit and display the data on a line plot
evidence: Measure the lengths of several objects and record the data
Create a line plot with a horizontal scale marked in whole-number units
Interpret a line plot to answer questions about the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the length of ten leaves to the nearest cm and records the results, can they display the data on a simple number-line plot — grouping leaves of the same length?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring with different units
topics.description: Measure the length of an object using two different length units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen
evidence: Measure a desk in both centimetres and inches and compare the two numbers
Explain that measuring with a smaller unit gives a larger number
Predict whether a measurement in centimetres will be greater or less than in inches
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the same book in centimetres and then in inches, can they explain why the numbers are different even though the book hasn't changed size?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to the minute (age 7+)
topics.description: Tell and write time from analogue and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m., p.m., and 12-hour and 24-hour notation
evidence: Read the time to five minutes on an analogue clock face
Write the time using digital notation (e.g. 3:25)
Distinguish between a.m. and p.m. and relate to daily events
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a clock shows 6:45 a.m., can {{name}} tell you what time that is in words — and write it in 24-hour notation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time Units and Calendar Facts
topics.description: Know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year, and leap year
evidence: State that there are 60 seconds in a minute
Name the months and state the number of days in each
Explain that a leap year has 366 days and occurs every 4 years
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} how many days are in September and whether this year is a leap year, can they answer both — and tell you how many seconds are in a minute?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 12-hour and 24-hour time
topics.description: Read, write, and convert time between analogue and digital 12-hour and 24-hour clocks
evidence: Convert 3:45 pm to 15:45 in 24-hour time
Read 19:30 and state the 12-hour equivalent as 7:30 pm
Match a set of 12-hour and 24-hour times
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a train timetable shows a departure at 14:35, can {{name}} convert that to 12-hour clock time — and tell you whether that's morning or afternoon?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area (age 8+)
topics.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft)
evidence: Count unit squares to find the area of an L-shaped figure
Measure the area of a book cover using square-centimetre tiles
Compare areas of two shapes by counting their unit squares
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a shape on squared centimetre paper, can they find its area by counting the squares — including making a sensible estimate for any partial squares?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and the distributive property
topics.description: Use tiling to demonstrate the distributive property: the area of a rectangle with sides a and (b+c) equals a×b + a×c; use area models to represent the distributive property
evidence: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle and show it decomposes into 3×4 and 3×2
Use an area model to compute 6×13 as 6×10 + 6×3
Draw an area model showing 5×(7+3) = 5×7 + 5×3
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to work out 6 × 13 by splitting it into 6 × 10 and 6 × 3, can they draw a rectangle divided into two parts to show why that method works?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area by Tiling
topics.description: Find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares and show that the result equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 4×6 rectangle and count 24 squares, then verify 4×6=24
Explain why the number of rows times the number in each row gives the area
Draw a rectangle on squared paper, tile it, and write the multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a rectangular room is 4 m long and 3 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area by tiling it with 1-metre squares in their head — and explain why that equals 4 × 3?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of compound shapes
topics.description: Recognise area as additive; find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing into non-overlapping rectangles and summing their areas
evidence: Decompose an L-shape into two rectangles, find each area, and add them
Find the area of a floor plan shaped like a T by splitting into rectangles
Solve: A room is L-shaped (3m×5m plus 2m×4m) — what is the total area?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped room on squared paper, can they split it into two rectangles, find the area of each part, and add them to get the total area?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting measurement units
topics.description: Convert between different units of measure (e.g. kilometre to metre, hour to minute, minute to second, year to month, week to day)
evidence: Convert 3 km to 3000 m
State 2 hours = 120 minutes
Convert 5 weeks to 35 days
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a journey is 3.5 km, can they convert that to metres — and also turn 2 hours 15 minutes into just minutes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating and comparing money
topics.description: Estimate, compare, and calculate different measures including money in pounds and pence
evidence: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres
Compare 1.5 kg and 1200 g and identify which is heavier
Calculate the total cost of 3 items at £2.45, £1.30, and £0.75
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing three items costing £2.85, £3.10, and £2.50, can they put them in order from cheapest to most expensive — and work out the total cost?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves and quarters (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch; display the data on a line plot with a scale marked in whole numbers, halves, and quarters
evidence: Measure five objects to the nearest 1/4 inch
Create a line plot showing the lengths of classmates' pencils in half-inches
Read a line plot and answer questions about the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures ten pencil lengths to the nearest quarter inch, can they record the data and plot it on a number line split into quarters — then spot which length appears most?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Liquids & Masses
topics.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using grams, kilograms, and litres; solve one-step word problems involving mass or volume
evidence: Estimate the mass of a textbook in grams or kilograms
Read a scale to measure liquid volume in litres
Solve: 3 bags weigh 250 g each — what is the total mass?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling bottles that each hold 250 ml from a 2-litre container of juice, can they work out how many bottles they can fill?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Solve word problems involving elapsed time by adding and subtracting time intervals in minutes, including using a number line
evidence: A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?
Calculate how many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05
Use a number line to show the elapsed time between two events
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts football practice at 3:20 p.m. and it lasts 75 minutes, can they work out what time it finishes — using a number line to help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeters of polygons
topics.description: Solve problems involving perimeters of polygons: find perimeter from side lengths, find an unknown side length, and explore rectangles with same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa)
evidence: Calculate the perimeter of a rectangle with sides 8 cm and 5 cm
Find the missing side of a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four known sides
Draw two rectangles both with perimeter 24 cm but different areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm and one side is 8 cm, can {{name}} work out the length of the other side — without drawing it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to the minute (age 8+)
topics.description: Tell and write time to the nearest minute using analogue and digital clocks
evidence: Read 7:43 from an analogue clock face
Write 11:06 on a digital display given a clock with hands
Match analogue and digital times to the nearest minute
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a clock's minute hand points just past the 9, can {{name}} work out the exact time to the nearest minute — and write it in digital format?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding angles (age 8+)
topics.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas
evidence: Calculate the area of a 7 cm × 9 cm rectangle as 63 cm²
Draw a rectangle with area 36 square units and label its side lengths
Solve: A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to carpet a room that is 5 m by 4 m, can they work out how much carpet to buy — using multiplication rather than counting squares?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding Area
topics.description: Understand that a unit square has one square unit of area and that the area of a plane figure is the number of unit squares that cover it without gaps or overlaps
evidence: Identify a unit square and state its area is 1 square unit
Explain why a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units
Distinguish between area and perimeter as different measurements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} counts the small squares inside a rectangle drawn on squared paper, can they tell you the area — and explain what "one square unit" means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting measurement units (age 9+)
topics.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min/sec); convert between different metric units and express measurements in terms of a smaller unit; record equivalents in conversion tables
evidence: Convert 3.5 km to 3,500 m
Complete a conversion table for cm and mm: (1,10), (2,20), (3,30)...
Express 2 kg 350 g as 2,350 g
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 3.5 kg to grams, can they do it confidently — and also fill in a simple two-column table showing the same measurements in kg and g?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating answers (age 9+)
topics.description: Apply the area formula (l × w) and perimeter formula (2l + 2w) for rectangles including squares in real-world and mathematical problems; calculate and compare areas using standard units (cm², m²) and estimate areas of irregular shapes
evidence: Find the width of a room given area = 48 m² and length = 8 m
Calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm
Estimate the area of an irregular pond drawn on a cm² grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to carpet a room 6.5 m × 4 m, can they calculate the area — and also work out how many metres of skirting board are needed around the edge?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating volume
topics.description: Estimate volume of cuboids using 1 cm³ blocks; estimate capacity of containers using water
evidence: Build a cuboid from 1 cm³ blocks and state its volume
Estimate how many cm³ blocks would fill a given box
Estimate the capacity of a jug by comparing to known litre measures
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a small cardboard box, can they estimate how many 1 cm³ cubes would fit inside it — and then fill it with sugar cubes to check?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Solve word problems involving distances, time intervals, liquid volumes, masses, and money using the four operations with fractions or decimals; represent with diagrams including number lines
evidence: A 2.5 kg bag of flour is split equally into 4 portions — what does each weigh?
A journey takes 1 hr 45 min; what time do you arrive if you leave at 09:20?
Three ribbons of 0.75 m, 1.2 m, and 0.95 m — what is the total length?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is planning a 4.5 km walk and has already walked 1.75 km, can they work out how far is left — and estimate how long the remaining walk might take?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement Line Plots
topics.description: Make a line plot to display measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions using line plot data
evidence: Create a line plot of seed growth measurements in 1/8-inch increments
Use a line plot to find the difference between the longest and shortest specimens
Calculate the total length of all items in a line plot by adding the fractional measurements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records caterpillar lengths as fractions of an inch and plots them on a number line, can they work out the total length of three caterpillars by adding the fractions from the plot?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Metric & Imperial Conversion
topics.description: Understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units (inches, pounds, pints)
evidence: State that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and use this to estimate length in inches
Know that 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds and estimate a person's weight in pounds
Convert approximately between litres and pints (1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a baby weighs 7 pounds, can they give a rough idea of that in kilograms — using the approximate conversion they know?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter of Compound Shapes
topics.description: Measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres
evidence: Find the perimeter of an L-shaped figure by identifying all side lengths
Calculate the perimeter of a composite shape where some sides must be deduced
Draw a composite rectilinear shape with a perimeter of 40 cm
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped garden plan with all the side measurements labelled, can they add all the sides together to find the total perimeter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to the minute (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving converting between units of time (hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days)
evidence: Convert 3 hours 25 minutes to 205 minutes
A programme lasts 150 seconds — express in minutes and seconds
How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 2 hours 35 minutes into just minutes, can they do it — and then convert 180 seconds into minutes and seconds?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms
topics.description: Calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles using formulae (A = b × h for parallelograms, A = ½ × b × h for triangles)
evidence: Calculate the area of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and height 5 cm
Calculate the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 7 cm
Explain why the area of a triangle is half the area of a related parallelogram
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is cutting triangular pieces of cloth where the base is 8 cm and the height is 5 cm, can they use a formula to work out the area of each piece?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Unit Cubes
topics.description: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and other units
evidence: Count unit cubes in a 3D diagram to determine volume in cm³
Measure the volume of a small container by filling it with centimetre cubes
Express a measured volume using the correct cubic unit notation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a 3-D shape built from small cubes in a diagram, can they count how many cubes it contains — even the ones hidden at the back — to find the volume?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system (e.g. 5 cm to 0.05 m) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places; convert between smaller and larger units of length, mass, volume, and time
evidence: Convert 3,250 g to 3.25 kg using decimal notation
Convert 0.45 km to 450 m
Explain the relationship between mm, cm, m, and km using powers of 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 5 cm to metres and write the answer as a decimal, can they do it — and also convert 2.45 kg into grams?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating answers (age 10+)
topics.description: Find the volume of right rectangular prisms by packing with unit cubes and show it equals l × w × h (or base area × height); apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h to solve real-world problems; calculate, estimate, and compare volumes of cubes and cuboids in standard units (cm³, m³)
evidence: Use V = l × w × h to find the volume of a cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm = 60 cm³
Explain why packing a prism with unit cubes gives the same result as multiplying edge lengths
Compare volumes of two cuboids and identify which has greater capacity
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to work out how much soil fits in a plant box that is 40 cm long, 20 cm wide, and 15 cm deep, can they use a formula to calculate the volume?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement Conversions
topics.description: Solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation and multi-step reasoning in real-world contexts
evidence: Solve: 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?'
Compare 2.5 litres and 2,450 ml by converting to the same unit
Solve a multi-step problem involving time, distance, and unit conversion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a fish tank that holds 60 litres and the tap fills it at 3.5 litres per minute, can they work out how long it will take to fill the tank?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise volume as an attribute of solid figures; understand that a unit cube (side length 1 unit) has 'one cubic unit' of volume and can be used to measure volume; a solid packed with n unit cubes has volume n cubic units
evidence: Explain what 'volume' means for a 3D shape and how it differs from area
Identify a unit cube and explain that it represents one cubic unit of volume
Determine the volume of a small solid by counting the unit cubes that fill it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a solid shape using small cubes, can they count the cubes to find the volume — and explain what "one cubic centimetre" means in everyday terms?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Miles & Kilometres
topics.description: Convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship (5 miles ≈ 8 km)
evidence: Convert 40 miles to approximately 64 km
Explain why the conversion factor between miles and km is approximately 1.6
Use the miles↔km relationship to compare a 10 km race with a 6-mile run
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is driving 40 miles to a theme park, can they use the rule that 5 miles ≈ 8 km to estimate roughly how many kilometres that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters and vice versa; explore this relationship systematically
evidence: Draw two rectangles with area 24 cm² but different perimeters
Find two shapes with perimeter 20 cm but different areas
Explain why a long thin rectangle and a square can have the same area but different perimeters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 12 square tiles to arrange, can they make different-shaped rectangles and notice that the area stays the same (12 tiles) but the perimeters are all different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume as additive
topics.description: Recognise volume as additive; find volumes of composite solid figures made of two or more non-overlapping right rectangular prisms
evidence: Decompose an L-shaped solid into two cuboids and calculate total volume
Solve a real-world problem requiring the volume of a composite figure (e.g. a step-shaped structure)
Explain why splitting a composite solid into rectangular prisms allows calculation of total volume
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an L-shaped swimming pool is made of two rectangular sections, can {{name}} find the volume of each section separately and add them to get the total volume of the pool?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as equal sharing
topics.description: Understand division as sharing equally into groups or as grouping (how many groups of a given size can be made)
evidence: Share 10 counters equally between 2 plates
Group 12 objects into sets of 3 and count 4 groups
Use concrete objects to solve 'How many groups of 2 in 8?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 12 grapes to share equally between 3 friends, can they work out that each friend gets 4 — and explain what they did?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication
topics.description: Use arrays to represent multiplication and division situations
evidence: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 objects to show 3 × 4
Read an array and state the total
Use an array to solve a simple division problem (e.g. 12 objects in rows of 4 → 3 rows)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees eggs arranged in 3 rows of 4 in a box, can they use that grid layout to work out both '3 × 4 = 12' and '12 ÷ 3 = 4'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition
topics.description: Understand multiplication as repeated addition and grouping equal sets
evidence: Explain that 3 groups of 2 is the same as 2 + 2 + 2
Use objects to make equal groups and count the total
Recognise an array as showing equal rows
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to count 4 bags with 3 apples in each, can they see that instead of counting all 12 one by one, they could add 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 — or say '4 groups of 3'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Commutative Multiplication
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of multiplication and recognise that division is not commutative
evidence: Explain that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 and show this with an array rotated
Use commutativity to choose the easier calculation
Demonstrate that 12 ÷ 3 ≠ 3 ÷ 12
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 4 × 7 gives the same answer as 7 × 4 — so they can choose whichever order is easier to remember from their times tables?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition (age 6+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and known facts
evidence: Solve 'There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples?' using repeated addition or known fact
Solve 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children' using grouping
Draw an array to solve a multiplication problem in context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} 'you have 5 bags with 4 marbles in each — how many altogether?', can they figure it out using objects, a drawing, or mental adding?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd and even numbers
topics.description: Recognise odd and even numbers
evidence: Identify whether a given number is odd or even
Explain that even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups
Spot the pattern: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a number like 37 or 84, can they quickly tell you whether it's odd or even — and explain how they know?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading ×, ÷, and = Symbols
topics.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols ×, ÷, and = in multiplication and division number sentences
evidence: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve'
Write a multiplication sentence to match an array
Read 12 ÷ 3 = 4 aloud correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you write '6 × 4 = 24' or '15 ÷ 3 = 5' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the times sign, division sign, and equals sign each mean?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5, and 10 multiplication tables
evidence: Quickly answer 5 × 3 = 15 from memory
Quickly answer 20 ÷ 5 = 4 from memory
Recite the 2, 5, and 10 times tables fluently
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall times table facts from the 2s, 5s, and 10s — like '5 × 6 = 30' or '20 ÷ 2 = 10' — forwards and backwards?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication (age 7+)
topics.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends
evidence: Count objects in a 3×4 array and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Explain that each row has the same number of objects so the total can be found by repeated addition
Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 4 rows of 5 stickers on a sheet, can they use repeated addition — '5 + 5 + 5 + 5' — to find the total, and write it as an equation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-Step Multiply & Divide
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division, including scaling problems and correspondence problems where n objects are connected to m objects
evidence: Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'the ribbon is 3 times as long')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '4 shirts and 3 trousers — how many outfits?')
Solve a missing-number multiplication or division problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe for 4 people needs 3 eggs, can {{name}} work out how many eggs are needed for 8 people — recognising it as a doubling or scaling problem?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rows & Columns in Rectangles
topics.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them
evidence: Divide a rectangle into equal rows and columns of unit squares
Count the total number of squares using repeated addition or skip counting
Relate the rows-and-columns structure to a rectangular array
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw lines to divide a rectangle into a neat grid of equal squares, then count all the squares to find the total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables (age 7+)
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4, and 8 multiplication tables
evidence: Recall 3 × 1 through 3 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 4 × 1 through 4 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 8 × 1 through 8 × 12 and corresponding division facts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts from the 3, 4, and 8 times tables — like '8 × 7 = 56' or '36 ÷ 4 = 9' — without having to work them out each time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Written Multiplication & Division
topics.description: Write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods
evidence: Calculate 23 × 4 using partitioning (20 × 4 + 3 × 4)
Calculate 96 ÷ 8 using known table facts
Begin to use a formal written layout for short multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '23 × 4' or '68 ÷ 4' — either in their head using times table knowledge, or by writing it out step by step?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: All times tables to 12×12
topics.description: Recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12
evidence: Recall any fact from the 1–12 times tables rapidly
Recall the corresponding division fact for any multiplication fact
Use known facts to check or derive answers in calculations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} recall any multiplication or division fact from all the times tables up to 12 — like '9 × 8 = 72' or '132 ÷ 12 = 11' — quickly and accurately?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as Unknown Factor
topics.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (e.g. find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8)
evidence: Explain that 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32

Use base-ten blocks to show a two-digit number as tens and ones
Identify the tens digit and ones digit in any two-digit number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 47, can they tell you there are 4 tens (forty) and 7 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'four seven'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 10 or 100 More or Less
topics.description: Find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number up to 1000
evidence: Given a three-digit number, state what is 10 more and 10 less
Given a three-digit number, state what is 100 more and 100 less
Explain the strategy using place-value understanding (e.g. only the tens/hundreds digit changes)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '10 more than 342' or '100 less than 875' in their head — knowing which digit changes and which stays the same?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: A Hundred Is Ten Tens
topics.description: Understand that 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a 'hundred'
evidence: Explain that 10 groups of 10 ones make 100
Bundle ten tens sticks into one hundred and describe what happened
Represent 100 using base-ten blocks showing 10 tens
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that ten full tens stacked together make one hundred — and that this is why 100 has a 1 in the hundreds place and zeros in the rest?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd or Even
topics.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members
evidence: Pair objects and determine whether there is one left over (odd) or not (even)
Count a group by 2s to determine if the total is even
Write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends (e.g. 8 = 4 + 4)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a group of 14 objects, can they tell you whether that number is odd or even — for example by pairing them up to see if any are left over?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering Numbers to 1000
topics.description: Compare and order numbers up to 1000 using >, =, and < symbols, based on place-value understanding
evidence: Compare two three-digit numbers by examining hundreds first, then tens, then ones
Use >, =, and < correctly to record comparisons of three-digit numbers
Order a set of numbers up to 1000 from smallest to largest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a set of three-digit numbers like 456, 231, and 789, can they put them in order and use > and < correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value to 1000
topics.description: Solve number problems and practical problems involving place value of numbers up to 1000
evidence: Solve a problem that requires identifying how many hundreds, tens, or ones are in a number
Apply place-value knowledge to a practical context (e.g. counting money in pounds)
Explain the strategy used to solve a place-value problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told 'I have 4 hundreds, 3 tens, and 7 ones — what number is that?', can they put it together and tell you 437?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 1000
topics.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 in numerals, number names, and expanded form
evidence: Read a three-digit numeral aloud correctly
Write a three-digit number in words (e.g. 'three hundred and forty-two')
Write a number in expanded form (e.g. 600 + 30 + 7)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 1,000 — both as numerals and in words — like reading '642' as 'six hundred and forty-two'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The multiples of 100
topics.description: Understand that the multiples of 100 (100–900) each represent a number of hundreds with 0 tens and 0 ones
evidence: Identify that 300 means 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones
Place multiples of 100 on a number line to 1000
Read and write multiples of 100 and explain their place-value structure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that 700 means 7 hundreds with no tens and no ones — and show what that looks like using base-ten blocks or a drawing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The three digits of a three-digit number
topics.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones
evidence: State the value of each digit in a three-digit number (e.g. in 362, the 3 represents 3 hundreds)
Partition a three-digit number into hundreds, tens, and ones (e.g. 485 = 400 + 80 + 5)
Explain why 706 has 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 348, can they tell you there are 3 hundreds, 4 tens, and 8 ones — rather than just reading the digits as 'three four eight'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 1000 More or Less
topics.description: Find 1000 more or less than a given number
evidence: Given 4,562, state that 1000 more is 5,562 and 1000 less is 3,562
Explain using place value that only the thousands digit changes
Apply this skill to numbers beyond 10,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '1,000 more than 3,456' or '1,000 less than 7,200' in their head — knowing only the thousands digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Large Numbers
topics.description: Order and compare numbers beyond 1000
evidence: Compare two four-digit numbers using >, <, and = by examining digits from the highest place value
Order a set of numbers up to 10,000 from smallest to largest
Justify the ordering using place-value reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} put a set of four-digit numbers like 4,321, 1,876, and 9,045 in order from smallest to largest — comparing them digit by digit?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Negative Numbers
topics.description: Count backwards through zero to include negative numbers
evidence: Count backwards from 5 through zero: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2 …
Place negative numbers on a number line
Understand that negative numbers are less than zero and use them in context (e.g. temperature)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count backwards past zero into negative numbers — like 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, −2, −3 — without hesitating at zero?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers to 10,000
topics.description: Identify, represent, and estimate numbers up to 10,000 using different representations
evidence: Represent a four-digit number on a place-value chart or with base-ten materials
Estimate where a number falls on a 0–10,000 number line
Match different representations of the same number (e.g. expanded form, place-value counters, numeral)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark a number like 6,400 roughly in the right place on a number line that goes from 0 to 10,000 — and explain how they decided where to put it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place value of each digit
topics.description: Recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number (thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones)
evidence: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number (e.g. in 7,345 the 7 represents 7 thousands)
Partition a four-digit number into thousands, hundreds, tens, and ones
Compose a four-digit number from given place-value parts (e.g. 3000 + 400 + 50 + 2 = 3,452)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the number 5,347, can they tell you the value of each digit — that the 5 means 5,000, the 3 means 300, the 4 means 40, and the 7 means 7?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value Problem-Solving
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving place value with increasingly large positive numbers
evidence: Solve a problem requiring rounding, comparing, or ordering numbers beyond 1000
Apply place-value knowledge in a practical context (e.g. population figures, distances)
Explain the strategy used, referencing place-value understanding
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked 'what is the largest 4-digit even number you can make from the digits 3, 7, 1, and 8?', can they work through it systematically and give you an answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman numerals to 100
topics.description: Read Roman numerals to 100 (I to C) and understand that the numeral system changed over time to include zero and place value
evidence: Read and write Roman numerals I, V, X, L, C and combinations up to 100
Convert between Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals (e.g. XLIV = 44)
Explain that Roman numerals have no zero and no place-value system
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like XIV (14) or XLII (42) — and do they know why we stopped using Roman numerals for most things once zero and place value were invented?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding to 10, 100, 1000
topics.description: Round any number to the nearest 10, 100, or 1000
evidence: Explain the rounding rule using a number line (which multiple is closer)
Apply rounding to estimate calculations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a number like 4,738 to the nearest 10 (4,740), 100 (4,700), or 1,000 (5,000) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 9+)
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000, 100,000) for any given number up to 1,000,000
evidence: Count on in 10,000s from 462,000
Count back in 100,000s from 800,000
Identify the next three terms: 375,000; 475,000; 575,000; ...
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count forwards and backwards in steps of 1,000 or 10,000 from any starting number — like 34,500, 44,500, 54,500 — without losing track?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Negative numbers in context
topics.description: Interpret negative numbers in context (temperature, sea level, bank balance); count forwards and backwards with positive and negative whole numbers, including through zero
evidence: Place –3, –1, 0, 2, 5 on a number line
The temperature is –4°C and rises by 7 degrees — what is the new temperature?
Count backwards from 3 in ones: 3, 2, 1, 0, –1, –2
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the temperature drops to −5°C overnight and rises to 3°C by day, can {{name}} place both on a number line and say how many degrees warmer the daytime temperature is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value × 10 Pattern
topics.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right (e.g. 700 ÷ 70 = 10)
evidence: Explain that the 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300
Complete: 700 ÷ 70 = __ and explain using place-value reasoning
State how many times greater the value of the 5 in 50,000 is than the 5 in 5,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 700, the 7 is worth 10 times more than in 70 — because moving one place to the left multiplies the value by 10?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers (age 9+)
topics.description: Read, write, order, and compare whole numbers up to at least 1,000,000 using base-ten numerals, number names, expanded form, and place-value understanding
evidence: Write 403,072 in words and in expanded form
Compare 548,301 and 543,801 using < and explain the reasoning
Order four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers into the millions — like 1,340,000 — and put a set of large numbers in order correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman numerals to 1000
topics.description: Read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals
evidence: Read MCMXCIX as 1999
Write 2024 in Roman numerals (MMXXIV)
Explain the subtractive principle: IV = 4 not IIII
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read Roman numerals like MMXIX (2019) or CDXLIV (444) — and recognise the year a film or building was made when it's shown in Roman numerals?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding Large Numbers
topics.description: Round any whole number up to 1,000,000 to the nearest 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000, or 100,000 using place-value understanding
evidence: Round 456,782 to the nearest 10,000 (460,000)
Round 950,500 to the nearest 100,000 and explain the boundary case
Use rounding to estimate the sum of 387,412 + 214,560
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a large number like 346,712 to the nearest 1,000 (347,000) or 10,000 (350,000) — identifying which digit to look at for each rounding?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Working with Large Numbers
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, and rounding whole numbers up to 1,000,000
evidence: What is the largest six-digit number with digits summing to 15?
A stadium holds 67,450 people. Round to the nearest thousand for a news report
Order the populations of five cities and find the difference between the largest and smallest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told the population of a city is 2,347,819, can they read that number aloud correctly and say roughly how many millions it is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Round decimals to any place using place-value understanding; round any whole number to a required degree of accuracy
evidence: Round 3.4567 to 2 decimal places (3.46)
Use rounding to estimate 4.83 × 2.17 ≈ 5 × 2 = 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} round a decimal like 3.748 to one decimal place (3.7) or two decimal places (3.75) — and explain which digit they look at to decide?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring temperature
topics.description: Use negative numbers in context (temperature, finance, sea level); calculate intervals across zero
evidence: The temperature falls from 3°C to −5°C — what is the drop? (8 degrees)
Calculate the difference between a bank balance of −£120 and £350
Order −7, −3, 0, 2, 5 on a number line and find the interval from −7 to 5
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bank account goes from −£45 to +£120, can {{name}} work out the total change — counting through zero to get £165?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers to Ten Million
topics.description: Solve number and practical problems involving reading, writing, ordering, comparing, rounding, and negative numbers up to 10,000,000
evidence: A country's population is 8,274,500 — round to the nearest million for a headline
Order the depths of three ocean trenches given in metres including negative values
Estimate the total attendance at three events by rounding each to the nearest 100,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that the distance to the Moon is about 384,400 km, can they round it to the nearest 10,000 km and say whether it's closer to 380,000 or 390,000?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Patterns with Powers of Ten
topics.description: Explain patterns in zeros when multiplying by powers of 10 and in decimal-point placement when multiplying/dividing by a power of 10; use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10 (e.g. 10³ = 1000)
evidence: Write 10⁴ = 10,000 and explain the exponent means four factors of 10
Explain why 3.4 × 10² = 340 by describing the decimal shift
Predict 2.56 × 10³ without calculating and explain the pattern
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain why 10² = 100 and 10³ = 1,000, and why multiplying by 10 just adds a zero — connecting the pattern of zeros to place value?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Place Value × 10 and ÷ 10
topics.description: Recognise that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left
evidence: Explain that the 4 in 0.04 is 1/10 of the 4 in 0.4
State that a digit moving one place left is ×10 and one place right is ÷10
Compare the value of the 6 in 6,000 and in 0.006
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that in 4.56, the digit 5 is worth 5 tenths — ten times less than the 5 in 54, and ten times more than the 5 in 0.056?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers (age 10+)
topics.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form; compare using >, =, < based on place-value meaning
evidence: Compare 0.372 and 0.38 using place-value reasoning
Write 'five and sixty-two thousandths' as 5.062
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write decimals like 3.047 or 0.625, say what each digit means (3 ones, 0 tenths, 4 hundredths, 7 thousandths), and put a set of decimals in order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading and writing numbers to 10,000,000
topics.description: Read, write, order, and compare numbers up to 10,000,000 and determine the value of each digit
evidence: Write 4,302,561 in words
Order four seven-digit numbers from smallest to largest
State the value of the 7 in 7,045,200 as seven million
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read and write numbers up to 10 million — like 4,302,617 — and say the value of any digit in the number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading Decimal Places
topics.description: Identify the value of each digit in numbers given to three decimal places (e.g. in 4.378, the 7 represents 7 hundredths)
evidence: State the value of each digit in 2.635 (2 ones, 6 tenths, 3 hundredths, 5 thousandths)
Explain the relationship between adjacent decimal places (each place is ten times smaller)
Write a number given digit values (e.g. 4 ones, 0 tenths, 7 hundredths, 3 thousandths = 4.073)
topics.assessmentPrompt: In the number 4.378, can {{name}} tell you that the 7 represents 7 hundredths — not 7 tenths or 7 thousandths?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Understand and use place value for decimals, measures, and integers of any size; extend the number system to include all positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a single number line
evidence: Identify the value of any digit in numbers of any size including decimals
Place positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line
Use place value to compare and order numbers across the full number system
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} place a mix of numbers — like 3, −2, 0.5, −1.75, and ¼ — all on the same number line, in the right order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line (age 11+)
topics.description: Order positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions on a number line; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values including negative numbers and mixed representations
evidence: Order a mixed set of positive and negative integers, decimals, and fractions
Use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly in mathematical statements
Compare numbers presented in different forms such as 0.75 and 3/4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a mixed list like 2.5, −3, ¾, 0, and −0.5, can they put them in order from least to greatest using a number line if needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from zero on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude in real-world contexts; distinguish absolute value comparisons from ordering statements
evidence: Define absolute value as distance from zero on a number line
Calculate the absolute value of positive and negative rational numbers
Distinguish between comparing absolute values and comparing signed numbers in real-world contexts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you that the absolute value of −7 is 7 — because it's 7 steps from zero on a number line regardless of direction — and use this idea to compare distances?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equally Likely Outcomes
topics.description: Understand that 'equally likely' means every outcome has exactly the same chance of occurring; identify whether a given situation has equally likely outcomes (a fair coin, a fair die, a spinner with equal sections) or unequally likely outcomes (a bag with more of one colour, a spinner with unequal sections)
evidence: Explain that a fair coin has equally likely outcomes because heads and tails each have the same chance
Identify whether a spinner with unequal sections has equally likely outcomes or not, and explain why
Give an example of a situation with equally likely outcomes and one without, explaining the difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell the difference between a fair situation — like rolling a normal die where every number has the same chance — and an unfair one, like a bag with many more of one colour than another?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Likelihood Language
topics.description: Use probability language to describe and compare the likelihood of everyday events using words such as certain, likely, even chance, unlikely, impossible
evidence: Place five everyday events (e.g. 'the sun will rise tomorrow', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads') on a scale from impossible to certain
Use 'likely', 'unlikely', 'certain', 'impossible', and 'even chance' correctly to describe different events
Explain why pulling a red ball from a bag of mostly red balls is 'likely' but not 'certain'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} use words like "certain," "likely," "unlikely," and "impossible" correctly — for example, knowing that rolling a 7 on a normal die is impossible but rolling an even number is likely?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ordering Likelihoods
topics.description: Compare the likelihood of different events and order them from least to most likely — including situations with unequal outcomes such as a bag with more of one colour than another, or a spinner with sections of different sizes — and explain reasoning using informal language
evidence: Order four or more events from least likely to most likely and justify each placement
Compare likelihoods when outcomes are not equally likely — e.g. 'Drawing red from a bag with 7 red and 3 blue is more likely than drawing blue'
Explain why some events are closer to 'even chance' and others are closer to 'certain' or 'impossible'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bag has 8 red counters and 2 blue ones, does {{name}} understand that picking red is much more likely than picking blue — and can they put different events in order from least to most likely?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Probability as a Fraction
topics.description: Describe the probability of simple equally-likely outcomes using unit fractions: the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6, flipping heads is 1/2, picking one specific colour from three equally represented colours is 1/3; place these fractional probabilities on a 0-to-1 probability scale
evidence: State that the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair die is 1/6 and explain why
Express the probability of picking a red card from a standard deck as 26/52 or 1/2
Write the probability of a simple event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a fair coin, do they know the probability of getting heads is 1/2 — and can they express similar simple probabilities as fractions and place them on a 0-to-1 scale?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple Chance Experiments
topics.description: Conduct simple probability experiments — flipping a coin, rolling a die, pulling coloured counters from a bag — record results, and compare experimental outcomes with expected theoretical outcomes
evidence: Flip a coin 20 times, record heads and tails in a tally chart, and describe what they notice about the results
Roll a die 30 times and compare how often each number came up with what they expected
Pull counters from a bag, record results, and explain whether the outcomes matched their prediction
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} ever done an experiment like flipping a coin or rolling a die lots of times, recorded the results in a tally chart, and noticed any patterns in what came up?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating Simple Probability
topics.description: Calculate the probability of a simple event with equally likely outcomes using the formula: probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes; express the result as a fraction in its simplest form; apply to rolling dice, drawing from bags, and other simple chance situations
evidence: Calculate the probability of drawing a blue marble from a bag of 3 blue and 7 red as 3/10
Use the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes to solve at least three different problems
Explain why increasing the number of favourable outcomes increases the probability
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are 3 red and 7 blue balls in a bag, can {{name}} work out the probability of picking a red one and express it as a fraction in its simplest form?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Experimental vs Theoretical
topics.description: Run repeated probability experiments and compare experimental (relative frequency) results with theoretical predictions; understand and demonstrate that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends towards the theoretical probability — and that short runs can give very different results
evidence: Roll a die 60 times and compare experimental frequencies with the expected 10 per number
Explain why experimental results don't exactly match theoretical predictions but get closer with more trials
Predict what would happen if the experiment were repeated 600 times instead of 60
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} flips a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads, do they understand why this doesn't mean heads is "more likely" — and that the more times you flip, the closer the results get to 50:50?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Probabilities Sum to One
topics.description: Understand that when all possible outcomes of a trial are listed, their probabilities must add up to 1; use this to find the probability of an event NOT happening: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); apply this shortcut to avoid counting all unfavourable outcomes directly
evidence: List all outcomes of spinning a 4-colour spinner and verify their probabilities add up to 1
Calculate P(not rolling a 3) as 1 − 1/6 = 5/6 using the complement rule
Spot an error in a probability table where the values don't sum to 1 and explain what's wrong
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the probability of it raining tomorrow is 0.3, can {{name}} work out the probability of it NOT raining — and explain why all probabilities in a situation must add up to 1?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: The 0-to-1 Probability Scale
topics.description: Understand probability as a measure expressed as a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain); place events on the probability scale; express probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages
evidence: Place events on a number line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), expressing positions as fractions or decimals
Explain that a probability of 0.5 means 'even chance' and connect this to the informal word 'likely'
Convert between informal language ('very unlikely') and a numerical position on the 0-to-1 scale
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal, and a percentage — for example, knowing that an even chance is ½, 0.5, and 50%?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar Models for Ratios
topics.description: Represent ratio and proportion problems using bar models (rectangular strips divided into equal parts labelled with quantities) and tape diagrams (segmented strips showing part-to-part and part-to-whole relationships); use these visual models to set up and solve unequal sharing, scaling, and percentage problems — drawing the diagram first, then reading off the answer
evidence: Draw a bar model to represent a ratio problem — e.g. sharing £20 in the ratio 3:2 by drawing 5 equal blocks
Use a bar model to solve a proportion problem and explain each step
Compare bar models with other representations (tables, double number lines) and explain when each is most useful
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to share 30 stickers between two friends in a 2:3 ratio, can they draw a bar model — splitting a strip into 5 equal boxes — and use it to work out each share without just guessing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Percentages (age 9+)
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
evidence: Explain the difference between a 'ratio' and a 'proportion' using a concrete example like mixing paint
Use 'per cent' correctly and convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages in context
Define 'scale factor' and use it to describe how a shape has been enlarged or reduced
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is sharing something 3 ways and 2 ways, can they explain the difference between a ratio (like 3:2) and a proportion (like 3 out of 5) — showing they know what each word means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating Percentages
topics.description: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
evidence: Calculate 15% of 360 by finding 10% and 5% and combining
Compare two discounts given as percentages of different original prices
Explain a strategy for finding any percentage of an amount using known percentage facts
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a jumper originally costs £40 and is 15% off, can {{name}} work out how much the discount is and what the sale price would be?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ratio Problems
topics.description: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
evidence: If the ratio of red to blue beads is 3:5 and there are 15 blue beads, find the number of red beads
Use multiplication facts to find the missing value: 'For every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; if there are 20 oranges, how many apples?'
Explain the multiplicative relationship between two quantities in a ratio context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 3 eggs for every 200g of flour, can {{name}} work out how many eggs would be needed for 600g of flour?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scale and similar shapes
topics.description: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
evidence: Find the missing side of a similar rectangle given a scale factor of 3
Determine the scale factor between two similar triangles from given side lengths
Use a scale factor to enlarge or reduce a shape and verify that all sides are in the same ratio
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 5 m, and a room measures 3.5 cm on the plan, can they work out the real length of the room?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
evidence: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5
Solve: 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam gets three times as many as Jo. If there are 30 altogether, how many does each get?'
Use fraction knowledge to explain why sharing in ratio 2:3 means one person gets 2/5 of the total
topics.assessmentPrompt: If three friends share a bag of 24 sweets so that one person gets twice as many as each of the others, can {{name}} work out how many each person receives?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: One Quantity as a Fraction
topics.description: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
evidence: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours (= 3/8)
Express a larger quantity as a fraction of a smaller one and explain why the result exceeds 1
Simplify the resulting fraction and interpret its meaning in the original context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 boys and 20 girls in a class, can {{name}} express the number of boys as a fraction of the whole class and say whether that fraction is less than or greater than a half?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Ratio Notation
topics.description: Use ratio notation to describe the relationship between two or more quantities, simplify ratios to their simplest form, and convert between ratio and fraction representations
evidence: Write a ratio from a word problem and simplify it (e.g. 12:8 = 3:2)
Convert a ratio to equivalent fractions of a whole (e.g. 3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5)
Simplify ratios involving decimals or fractions by finding a common multiplier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a smoothie recipe uses orange juice and mango juice in the ratio 3:2, can {{name}} simplify that ratio, express it as a fraction, and work out how much of each is needed for a given total amount?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unit Conversions
topics.description: Convert freely between related standard units of measurement (time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places where appropriate
evidence: Convert between area units such as cm² and m² using the square of the linear scale factor
Perform multi-step conversions (e.g. convert 2.5 hours to seconds via minutes)
Convert volume units such as cm³ to litres and explain the relationship
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} convert between units confidently — for example, changing kilometres to metres, kilograms to grams, or hours and minutes to just minutes — including multi-step problems?
